seoDescription: Learn the essential technique for creating a professional-grade offset mold using sheet wax, a crucial step for manufacturing perfectly fitting composite cover components like a carbon fiber frame protector. This guide walks you through applying pliable, self-adhesive sheet wax to an original part to create a slightly larger mold. This offset ensures your final part will fit precisely over the original shape. The process covers everything from wax application and joining techniques to building the mold with epoxy tooling gel coat and putty reinforcement.

chapters.title: Introduction to Offset Molds for Cover Components
chapters.description: Learn why a standard mold won't work for cover components and how an offset mold provides the necessary clearance.

chapters.title: Understanding and Preparing Sheet Wax
chapters.description: Discover the properties of self-adhesive sheet wax and how to measure and cut it for your project.

chapters.title: Applying and Shaping the Sheet Wax
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to use a heat gun to form the sheet wax over complex curves and reinforce the mold flanges.

chapters.title: How to Create a Seamless Join in Sheet Wax
chapters.description: Learn a professional technique for seamlessly joining two pieces of sheet wax on larger or more complicated shapes.

chapters.title: Preparing the Pattern for Mold Making
chapters.description: The frame is masked for protection and the contents of the epoxy mold making starter kit are introduced.

chapters.title: Mixing and Applying the First Gel Coat Layer
chapters.description: This chapter covers the correct mixing and application technique for the first layer of epoxy tooling gel coat.

chapters.title: Applying the Second Gel Coat Layer
chapters.description: Learn how to check the tackiness of the first coat before applying a second layer of gel coat for a robust mold surface.

chapters.title: Reinforcing the Mold with Epoxy Putty
chapters.description: This chapter shows how to mix and apply epoxy mold making putty to reinforce the gel coat and build the mold's structure.

chapters.title: Demolding and Removing the Sheet Wax
chapters.description: After a full cure, the mold is removed from the part and the sheet wax is carefully scraped out and cleaned from the mold surface.

chapters.title: Polishing the Mold for a Gloss Finish
chapters.description: Transform the satin mold surface into a high-gloss finish by wet-sanding and polishing with compound.

chapters.title: Conclusion and Next Steps
chapters.description: A final look at the completed, polished offset mold and a preview of the next video on making the carbon fiber part.

summary:
## The Need for an Offset Mold

When creating a cover or protector for an existing component, a mold taken directly from the original part will produce a final piece that is too small on its inside dimension to fit. To solve this, you must create an **offset mold**.

*   An **offset mold** is slightly larger than the original part.
*   This extra space, or **offset**, accommodates the thickness of the final composite part, ensuring it fits perfectly over the original component.
*   For this project, a **2mm offset** is created, allowing for a part up to 2mm thick.

## Using Sheet Wax to Create the Offset

**Sheet wax** is the ideal material for creating the offset on the original part (the pattern) before making the mold.

*   **Key Properties:** It's a pliable sheet of wax with a **self-adhesive backing**, available in various thicknesses to match your desired offset.
*   **Application Process:**
    *   Cut the sheet wax oversized to include material for the mold's **flanges**.
    *   Use a **hairdryer or heat gun** to soften the wax, making it easy to conform to complex curves.
    *   Firmly press the wax onto the pattern surface.

> [!TIP]
> **To seamlessly join two pieces of sheet wax:** Overlap the new piece on the existing one and press firmly to create a witness mark. Cut along the mark on the new piece for a perfect butt joint. Seal the tiny gap by rubbing **filleting wax** into the seam and scraping it flush.

## Building the Epoxy Mold

Once the sheet wax pattern is complete, you can begin building the mold.

### 1. Gel Coat Application

*   The mold surface is created with **epoxy tooling gel coat**.
*   Apply the first coat evenly, aiming for a thickness of about **500g per square meter**.
*   Allow the gel coat to cure for several hours until it's tacky but does not transfer to your glove.
*   Apply a second, identical coat of gel coat to build a robust and durable mold surface.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> No release agent is necessary when applying epoxy gel coat directly onto sheet wax. The epoxy will not bond to the wax, ensuring a clean release.

### 2. Reinforcement Layer

*   With the second gel coat layer still tacky, apply the reinforcement material.
*   For small molds, **epoxy mold making putty** is a convenient choice. It contains **chopped glass fibers** for strength and conforms easily to details.
*   Apply the putty in small pieces, pressing firmly to eliminate trapped air.
*   Build up a consistent thickness of **10-15mm** for structural rigidity.

> [!NOTE]
> For larger molds (over 0.5 sq meters), it is more cost-effective to use traditional **glass fiber cloth and epoxy laminating resin** for reinforcement after the gel coat has been applied.

## Finishing the Mold

### 1. Demolding and Cleaning

*   Allow the mold to **fully cure for 24 hours** at room temperature.
*   Carefully demold by peeling the new mold off the pattern.
*   Remove the sheet wax from the mold's surface using a **plastic scraper**. Gently warming the wax with a heat gun will make it more pliable and easier to remove.
*   Use a **mold cleaner** and a cloth to remove any final wax residue.

### 2. Achieving a Gloss Finish

The surface created by sheet wax has a satin texture. To produce gloss-finished parts, the mold itself must be polished to a high gloss.

*   **Wet-sand** the mold surface, starting with 1200-grit paper and progressing to 1500-grit.
*   **Polish** the sanded surface using a high-quality polishing compound (like NW1) until you achieve a smooth, mirror-like finish.
transcription:
## Introduction to Offset Molds for Cover Components

Hi, I'm Paul from Easy Composites and today I'll be showing you how you can use sheet wax to produce a mold for a properly fitting cover component such as this carbon fiber frame protector. I'll show you how to apply the sheet wax to the original part and then use this to create an offset mold that's slightly larger than that original part. In a later tutorial, we'll use this mold to make the frame protector itself.

There are many instances where you might want to make a cover or a protector for an existing component. This might be a clutch protector or an exhaust shield on a motorcycle. It could be sill protectors or interior trim pieces on a car. The example we're using today is this carbon fiber frame protector.

You might assume that to make a mold for a cover component is simply a case of taking a mold from the original shape and then using that to create the part. However, if you were to do this, the part that you made would actually be too small on the inside to fit back over the original shape. So, we need to make a mold which is larger. So, if we take a look at the example mold, you'll see that it is slightly larger than the part itself. And this is what's called an offset.

We can see that we have a 2 mm offset all the way around this part. So, there's a gap that runs right the way around. And that will mean that we can make a part inside this mold which is up to 2 mm thick from the surface and it will still fit over the original shape.

## Understanding and Preparing Sheet Wax

The easiest way to create an offset on your mold is to use sheet wax. Here at Easy Composites, we carry a range of different thicknesses suitable for creating different offsets depending on what you need. For this project, we'll be using the 2 mm sheet wax. So, the sheet wax is literally just that. It's a sheet of wax. The reverse side has a self-adhesive backing, which means you can apply it directly onto your part. And it's very, very pliable. And with some heat, it can follow compound curves quite easily.

So now we're just going to measure up and get the dimensions for this frame protector. We will cut the sheet wax larger because we're also going to use the sheet wax for the flanges. You'll see that in a moment. So 300 mm in length for the final guard and approximately 100 mm in width. So we'll just oversize that slightly. 

Here I'm marking out and cutting the sheet wax to the size of the surface plus a border that will provide the additional material to form the flange. Using a straight edge and a sharp knife easily cuts the wax.

## Applying and Shaping the Sheet Wax

To form the sheet wax, you can do quite a lot by hand and it will follow the curves quite easily, but using a hairdryer or a heat gun will make it more pliable for complicated areas.

The overhang from the sheet wax here is going to form the flange of the mold. But because this material is quite pliable, I'm going to add some filing wax just onto the underside to give them a bit more stability.

## How to Create a Seamless Join in Sheet Wax

For this job, it's been perfectly practical to do this in one piece. So, here we've got no joins, but on larger or more complicated shapes, you might have to create a join in the sheet wax. I'm just going to quickly show you how that's done neatly.

This curved cut is made as an example of the sort of edge that you might need to make a joint against.

The second piece of material is cut oversized and overlaps the piece that you're wanting to join to. If you then press the sheet firmly against the underlying piece, this will make an impression in the sheet and witness through, making visible the precise position of where the cut needs to be made.

After making the cut and removing the excess material, any slight gaps remaining can be closed up by firmly pushing and sliding the pieces together.

To seal the joint, filleting wax is rubbed into the joint and then the joint is scraped back to level it out and remove any burring. Finally, a buff over with a cloth will leave you with an almost seamless finish.

## Preparing the Pattern for Mold Making

Now that the sheet wax is applied, I'm just going to mask off the rest of the frame to protect it from any splashes of gel coat.

To produce a small mold like this. All of the materials that are required are included in our mold making starter kit. So, that's what we're going to use for this project. Inside the kit, we have the epoxy tooling gel coat and hardener, the epoxy mold making putty and its hardener. Then, we have laminating brushes, some nitral gloves, mixing sticks and cups. And also included in the kit is mold release wax and PVA release agent.

## Mixing and Applying the First Gel Coat Layer

Now, we won't be using those today, but generally when you're making a mold, you would be doing. As with any epoxy resin, accurate weighing and thorough mixing is essential to ensure a proper and complete cure. For this mold, we will be doing two gel coat applications. So, I'll be using half of the 200 g pot for each.

When you mix the hardener into the gel coat, you need to do this very steadily so you don't whisk air in. It also needs to be very thoroughly mixed. So that would normally take probably three or four minutes on a batch like this.

As with all epoxies, it's really important to scrape the sides and bottom to make sure that you don't have any unmixed resins stuck in those areas.

You may have noticed that we haven't used any release agent. That's because with epoxy resin and sheet wax, it's not necessary. You will get a good release anyway.

The gel coat is applied with a thick and even coat. The technique involves using slow brush strokes with a heavily loaded brush. A sort of halfway between spreading and painting.

On flatter surfaces, often a single thick application of gel coat is all that's needed, but generally for most molds, two coats of gel is preferred. The aim here is to apply as thick a coat as you can without the gel starting to slump or drain from the steeper or vertical surfaces. This will normally equate to around 500 g per square meter per coat.

You should also take care to ensure that the coat is even and not to have any areas with pools of gel coat as these will shrink excessively during cure and could cause slight distortions on the final mold.

## Applying the Second Gel Coat Layer

We've left the first application of gel coat to tack off. That's taken 3 hours in our case. It will vary a bit depending on room temperature. The important thing is that the gel still has a good level of tack to allow the next layer to bond. To identify if you're at the right level of tack, you'll feel the surface is still very sticky, but none of the gel coat comes off on your finger when you do that.

The second application is done in exactly the same way as the first coat. It is worth pointing out that although we are using this project to demonstrate our small mold making kit, we do have all of these materials available individually and in bulk quantities on our website. And of course, this is only one of the many mold making solutions that Easy Composites offers.

## Reinforcing the Mold with Epoxy Putty

With the second gel at the same tacky stage, we're ready to go on with the reinforcement. The reinforcement that comes in the starter kit is an epoxy mold making putty or paste. Now, this is a very convenient material for making small molds like this as it conforms to the details in the corners very easily.

The epoxy mold making putty is essentially made up from a resin and filler and then for the reinforcement, there are chopped glass fibers in there. So, that's where the strength of the mold comes from. Just like epoxy resin, this needs to be combined with a hardener. And that does need to be done at an accurate ratio. But because I'm using all of this material, these are already pre-measured. So, I'm just going to mix the entire contents of the hardener into the paste.

To mix the hardener into the putty, it's just done by hand. And the blue color in the hardener helps to identify when it's been fully blended.

So once you're happy that the mix is thorough and consistent, the easiest way to work with this material is to spread it out into an area that's roughly the same size as the mold you're going to be working from and then divide this up into small pieces and apply them to the mold itself.

The reason for using small pieces is that when you apply this, it's much easier for any air that would be trapped underneath to escape as you're going. It's simply a case of pressing the material onto the surface and working over it.

On a mold like this, you're looking to get an overall thickness of between 10 and 15 mm.

This paste system is best suited to smaller molds of up to around half a square meter. Beyond this, it would generally be more cost effective and practical to use glass cloth and epoxy laminating resin to provide the primary enforcement after the gel. In these instances, it can be useful to use the putty in combination to help with filling sharp corners or getting into finer details that might be tricky to laminate with glass.

## Demolding and Removing the Sheet Wax

With the gel coat backed up with reinforcement, we're now going to leave this to fully cure, which is 24 hours at room temperature. We're now 24 hours on, and this mold is fully cured, so it's ready for removal. So, first of all, we'll just get rid of some of this masking tape.

We should be able to remove the mold by just applying a firm pressure and peeling it away from the frame.

So, there we go. And that's the sheet wax there inside.

the filleting wax. We can actually reuse this, so we'll save this for another project.

So, here we have the sheet wax, which is still stuck to the surface of the mold. To remove this, we're going to use a plastic scraper. So, we're using a demolding wedge, which is particularly suitable cuz it won't scratch the mold and it's got a nice sharp leading edge.

Sometimes you might find that sheet wax cracks when you're trying to remove it, especially if you're working in a cold environment. If you use a haird dryer or a heat gun to gently warm the wax, it will make it more pliable.

Even after thoroughly scraping the surface, we are still left with some traces of wax. So, we're going to remove those with a mold cleaner.

## Polishing the Mold for a Gloss Finish

So, you can see here the finish that we're left with directly from the sheet wax. Now, it's not a perfect surface finish. It does have very slight texture to it, and it's it sort of gives a satin finish. If you want a gloss finished part, you need to get a gloss finish onto your mold. To do that, we're going to flat this surface down with a fine wet and dry paper, and then go on to polish that with a polishing compound.

It is perfectly possible to polish straight from a 1200 grit finish, but actually if you go on to a 1500 grit, you'll find the polishing is quite a lot faster.

And now for the final polish, we're going to be using the NW1 polishing compound.

For larger molds, you'd probably use a machine buffer for polishing the surface, but on something like this, it's more than possible to do it by hand. The NW1 compound that we're using here is actually self-de-finishing, meaning as you're working it, it gets finer and finer on the grade, leaving a really fine gloss, but still able to get out those 1500 grit scratches at the beginning.

## Conclusion and Next Steps

This is the completed mold ready to be put into service. I hope this video has helped to explain just how easy it is to create an offset mold using sheet wax. If you want to see this mold being put to use, we have a following video where we use a simple wet lay and vacuum bagging technique to produce this carbon fiber frame protector.

If you're interested in finding out more about the materials and equipment we've used, visit the Easy Composites website where you'll find an extensive range of composite materials. And as ever, we always appreciate a like and a subscribe.
